17/02/2025, 09:45 - Kannan: PAPER  1
17/02/2025, 09:45 - Kannan: Abstract 

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) causes severe disability and death of young men because of
progressive muscle degeneration aggravated by sterile inflammation. DMD is also associated with
cognitive and bone-function impairments. This complex phenotype results from the cumulative loss of a
spectrum of dystrophin isoforms expressed from the largest human gene. Although there is evidence for
the loss of shorter isoforms having impact in the central nervous system, their role in muscle is unclear.
We found that at 8 weeks, the active phase of pathology in dystrophic mice, dystrophin-null mice
(mdxbgeo) presented with a mildly exacerbated phenotype but without an earlier onset, increased serum
creatine kinase levels, or decreased muscle strength. However, at 12 months, mdxbgeo diaphragm
strength was lower, whereas fibrosis increased, compared with mdx. The most striking features of the
dystrophin-null phenotype were increased ectopic myofiber calcification and altered macrophage
infiltration patterns, particularly the close association of macrophages with calcified fibers. Ectopic
calcification had the same temporal pattern of presentation and resolution in mdxbgeo and mdx muscles,
despite significant intensity differences across muscle groups. Comparison of the rare dystrophin-null
patients against those with mutations affecting full-length dystrophins may provide mechanistic in-
sights for developing more effective treatments for DMD
17/02/2025, 09:45 - Kannan: INTRODUCTION 

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severely debili-
tating and invariably fatal X-linked neuromuscular disorder,
which results from mutations in the DMD gene.1 DMD is
the largest human gene known, encoding multiple struc-
turally diverse isoforms of dystrophin.2 Three full-length
transcripts, comprising 79 exons, encode 427-kDa proteins
while further intragenic promoters3 drive expression of
progressively truncated variants (Figure 1A).
The current central hypothesis states that Duchenne
muscular dystrophy pathology is caused by the loss of the
full-length dystrophin (Dp427) in myofibers, where it an-
chors the dystrophin-associated protein complex, linking theextracellular matrix, the sarcolemma, and the intracellular
cytoskeleton. This assembly is considered critical for muscle
function and survival. Therefore, all the current preclinical
and clinical therapeutic approaches are aimed at dystrophin
restoration in differentiated muscle cells.
However, there is growing evidence that DMD mutations
produce a range of significant cell-autonomous abnormal-
ities in both human and mouse myogenic cells, suggesting a
much earlier onset of pathology and explaining impaired
muscle regeneration.4e10
The severity of DMD-associated cognitive impairment
correlates with the cumulative loss of dystrophin isoforms
expressed in the central nervous system, thus suggesting a
prominent functional role for these shorter isoforms in
brain cells.11,12 However, little attention has been given to
the potential role of shorter dystrophins controlled by the
intergenic promoters, and few in-depth comparisons be-
tween the full-length and the dystrophin-null muscle
phenotypes have been undertaken. Interestingly, the pro-
portion of patients with a severe motor and cognitive
phenotype has been shown to correlate with mutations
affecting all dystrophins.13 Gene mutations causing DMD
disrupt the reading frame and include large deletions
(68%), duplications (11%), and smaller rearrangements
and point mutations (20%).14 Initial analyses indicated that
the DMD gene mutation hot spots are located in the re-
gions encoding the full-length isoforms. However,
although large deletions and duplications have a
nonrandom distribution with the two identifiable hot spots,
small insertions/deletions and point mutations are distrib-
uted along the entire gene,15 thus affecting multiple
isoforms.
Interestingly, there are little data documenting the
expression of the so-called nonmuscle dystrophin isoforms
in muscle. Given that myogenic cells are affected by DMD
mutations and are known to express some of these truncated
isoforms (eg, Dp71), we hypothesized that null DMD mu-
tations may alter functions of myogenic cells and thus affect
the phenotype. Therefore, the consequences of total loss of
DMD expression were investigated. The muscle pathology
was compared in the most widely used animal model of
DMDdthe mdx mouse, lacking full-length isoforms
because of a point mutation in exon 23,16 against the
mdxbgeo dystrophin-null mouse with the reading-frame
disruption downstream of exon 63, which is present in all
dystrophins and therefore with all isoforms being ablated.
This mouse, unlike models generated by chemical muta-
genesis, is a true pan-dystrophin knockout with no revertant
fibers present.

17/02/2025, 09:54 - Kannan: PAPER 2
17/02/2025, 09:55 - Kannan: ABSTRACT 

Cardiac valve calcification and vascular calcification (VC) are
associated with cardiovascular mortality in the general population and in
patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD, diabetes mellitus, and ath-
erosclerosis are among the causes of systemic inflammation that are associ-
ated with VC.
Areas covered: This review collates clinical and experimental evidence that
inflammation accelerates VC progression. Specifically, we review the actions
of key pro-inflammatory cytokines and inflammation-related transcription fac-
tors on VC, and the role played by senescence. Inflammatory cytokines, such as
the TNF superfamily and IL-6 superfamily, and inflammation-related transcrip-
tion factor NF-kB promote calcification in cultured vascular smooth muscle
cells, valvular interstitial cells, or experimental animal models through direct
effects, but also indirectly by decreasing circulating Fetuin A or Klotho levels.
Expert opinion: Experimental evidence suggests a causal link between inflam-
mation and VC that would change the clinical approach to prevention and
treatment of VC. However, the molecular basis remains unclear and little is
known about VC in humans treated with drugs targeting inflammatory cyto-
kines. The effect of biologicals targeting TNF-a, RANKL, IL-6, and other
inflammatory mediators on VC, in addition to the impact of dietary phos-
phate in patients with chronic systemic inflammation, requires study.

17/02/2025, 10:02 - Kannan: TITLE

Mechanisms of ectopic calcification: implications for diabetic 
vasculopath
17/02/2025, 10:02 - Kannan: ABSTRACT 

 Vascular calcification (VC) is the deposition of calcium/phosphate in the vasculature, which 
portends a worse clinical outcome and predicts major adverse cardiovascular events. VC is an active 
process initiated and regulated via a variety of molecular signalling pathways. There are mainly two types 
of calcifications: the media VC and the intima VC. All major risk factors for cardiovascular disease (CVD) 
have been linked to the presence/development of VC. Besides the risk factors, a genetic component is also 
operative to determine arterial calcification. Several events take place before VC is established, including 
inflammation, trans-differentiation of vascular cells and homing of circulating pro-calcific cells. Diabetes is 
an important predisposing factor for VC. Compared with non-diabetic subjects, patients with diabetes show 
increased VC and higher expression of bone-related proteins in the medial layer of the vessels. In this review 
we will highlight the mechanisms underlying vascular calcification in diabetic patients.

17/02/2025, 11:43 - Kannan: ♦️PAPER 4
17/02/2025, 11:49 - Kannan: TITLE 

Plaque Calcification During Atherosclerosis Progression and 
Regressio
17/02/2025, 11:50 - Kannan: ABSTRACT 

Plaque calcification develops by the inflammation-dependent mechanisms involved in progression 
and regression of atherosclerosis. Macrophages can undergo two distinct polarization states, that is, 
pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype in progression and anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype in regression. 
In plaque progression, predominant M1 macrophages promote the initial calcium deposition within 
the necrotic core of the lesions, called as microcalcification, through not only vesicle-mediated min-
eralization as the result of apoptosis of macrophages and vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), but 
also VSMC differentiation into early phase osteoblasts. On the other hand, in plaque regression M2 
macrophages are engaged in the healing response to plaque inflammation. In association with the 
resolution of chronic inflammation, M2 macrophages may facilitate macroscopic calcium deposition, 
called as macrocalcification, through induction of osteoblastic differentiation and maturation of 
VSMCs. Oncostatin M, which has been shown to promote osteoblast differentiation in bone, may 
play a pivotal role in the development of plaque calcification. Clinically, two types of plaque calcifica-
tion have distinct implications. Macrocalcification leads to plaque stability, while microcalcification 
is more likely to be associated with plaque rupture. Statin therapy, which reduces cardiovascular mor-
tality, has been shown to exert its dual actions on plaque morphology, that is, regression of atheroma 
and increment of macroscopic calcium deposits. Statins may facilitate the healing process against 
plaque inflammation by enhancing M2 polarization of macrophages. Vascular calcification has pleio-
tropic properties as pro-inflammatory “microcalcification” and anti-inflammatory “macrocalcifica-
tion”. The molecular mechanisms of this process in relation with plaque progression as well as plaque 
regression should be intensively elucidated.

17/02/2025, 16:29 - Kannan: NOTES PAPER 4


Vascular calcification is an active and regulated process similar to bone formation.
Inflammation plays a key role in all stages of atherosclerosis and certain immune cells like macrophages influence the type of calcification that occurs.
 There are two types of calcification,microcalcification which is small deposition occur during plaque progression and promoted by M1 macrophage and there is microcalcification which is larger deposition,occurs during plaque regression and associated with M2 macrophage.
Oncostatin have dual role ,it helps macrophages switch to M2 macrophages which is an anti inflammatory state,it promotes bone like calcification,which means it encourages microcalcification,believe to make stable plaques that are less likely to rupture,reducing risk of heart attack.
Similarly statin (cholesterol lowering drug) encourages M2 macrophages and lead to macrocalcification.
Both OSM and statins help turn harmful small calcium deposits into larger, stable ones, which may be protective rather than dangerous.

Oncostatin have dual role it helps macrophage switch to M2 which is an anti -inflammatory state,it promotes bone like calcification mainly Macrocalcification, similarly statin a cholestrol lowering drug encourages M2 macrophages and lead Macrocalcification.

21/02/2025, 11:58 - Kannan: #PAPER 5
21/02/2025, 11:58 - Kannan: TITLE 

Osteogenesis Associates With Inflammation in Early-Stage
Atherosclerosis Evaluated by
Molecular Imaging In Vivo
21/02/2025, 11:58 - Kannan: ABSTRACT 


Calcification is a characteristic feature of atherosclerosis
and is predictive of cardiovascular events.1 Clinicopath-
ological studies suggest that atherosclerotic plaques are prone
to rupture at interface areas between high- and low-density
tissue, particularly in the superficial nodules of calcium
deposition.2– 4 In addition, microcalcification in the thin
fibrous cap may cause microfractures that lead to plaque
rupture and acute cardiovascular events.5 Furthermore, calci-
fication impacts clinical outcome not only by complicating
atherosclerosis but also by impairing the movement of aortic
valve leaflets,6 increasing arterial stiffness, which in turn
affects cardiac function,7 or by causing plaque fracture during
angioplasty.8,9
21/02/2025, 11:58 - Kannan: AUTHOR 

Elena Aikawa, MD, PhD; Matthias Nahrendorf, MD; Jose-Luiz Figueiredo, MD; Filip K. Swirski, PhD;
Timur Shtatland, PhD; Rainer H. Kohler, PhD; Farouc A. Jaffer, MD, PhD;
Masanori Aikawa, MD, PhD; Ralph Weissleder, MD, PhD
21/02/2025, 11:58 - Kannan: YEAR

2007
21/02/2025, 11:58 - Kannan: DOCUMENT 

Research article

21/02/2025, 11:58 - Kannan: NOTES

Arterial calcification is arteries getting clogged up with calcium, leading to heart attack and strokes
Scientist had a doublt about whether calcium build up is reason of inflammation and immune system activity.
Used mice with a atherosclerosis and used special glowing dyes to track inflammation and calcium deposits over time.
The used glowing dye that sticks to calcium and another dye that stick to macrophage.
They found out inflammation triggers calcification, inflammation is macrophages showing up in large number.
Special dye could detect the early stages of calcification.
Macrophage makes artery cells act like bone cells by release of certain chemicals, smooth muscles will start to behave like bone cells.
Since inflammation plays a big role,angi inflammatory drug could slow down the process.

21/02/2025, 12:13 - Kannan: #####PAPER 6

TITLE 

Calcification in atherosclerosis: Bone biology and chronic
inflammation at the arterial crossroads <This message was edited>
21/02/2025, 12:13 - Kannan: AUTHOR

Terence M. Doherty*, Kamlesh Asotra*, Lorraine A. Fitzpatrick†, Jian-Hua Qiao*, Douglas J. Wilkin*, Robert C. Detrano‡,
Colin R. Dunstan§, Prediman K. Shah*, and Tripathi B. Rajavashisth*
21/02/2025, 12:13 - Kannan: ABSTRACT 

Dystrophic or ectopic mineral deposition occurs in many pathologic conditions, including atherosclerosis. Calcium mineral deposits that fre-
quently accompany atherosclerosis are readily quantifiable radiographically, serve as a surrogate marker for the disease, and predict a
higher risk of myocardial infarction and death. Accelerating research interest has been propelled by a clear need to understand how
plaque structure, composition, and stability lead to devastating cardiovascular events. In atherosclerotic plaque, accumulating evidence is
consistent with the notion that calcification involves the participation of arterial osteoblasts and osteoclasts. Here we summarize current
models of intimal arterial plaque calcification and highlight intriguing questions that require further investigation. Because atherosclerosis
is a chronic vascular inflammation, we propose that arterial plaque calcification is best conceptualized as a convergence of bone biology
with vascular inflammatory pathobiology.
21/02/2025, 12:13 - Kannan: SPECIES 

mouse,human,mice
21/02/2025, 12:13 - Kannan: NOTES 

Arteries getting clogged with fat deposit is arthersclerosis.Structure and composition of plaques play a big role in how disease affect people .
Calcification was thought as a damage repair,but now found out as an active and regulated process, similar to how bone forms.
Osteoblast and osteoclast may be involved in calcification in arteries ,means calcification is linked with bone biology and chronic inflammation.
Presence of calcium in plaque help doctors predict risk of heart attack.

03/03/2025, 08:11 - Gokul G J: ശ്രീവല്ലഭക്ഷേത്രത്തിൽ ആനയിടഞ്ഞു, ഭയപ്പെടേണ്ട സാഹചര്യമില്ല

തിരുവല്ല: ശ്രീവല്ലഭ ക്ഷേത്രത്തില്‍ ഉത്സവ എഴുന്നള്ളത്തിനിടയില്‍ ആനവിരണ്ട് കൂട്ടാനയെകുത്തി . ഉത്സവത്തോട് അനുബന്ധിച്ച് എഴുന്നള്ളത്തിന് വന്ന വേണാട്ട് മറ്റം ഉണ്ണിക്കുട്ടന്‍ എന്ന മോഴയാനയാണ് വിരണ്ടത്. 

ഈ ആന ഒപ്പമുണ്ടായിരുന്ന തിരുവല്ല ദേവസ്വത്തിന്റെ ജയരാജനെ കുത്തി. അല്പം മുന്നോട്ട് കുതിച്ച ജയരാജന്‍ പഴയ ഊട്ടുപുരയ്ക്ക് സമീപത്തേക്ക് ഓടി.

 മുകളിലുണ്ടായിരുന്ന കീഴ്ശാന്തി താഴെക്ക് വീണെങ്കിലും ആനശാന്തനായതിനാല്‍ അപകടം ഒഴിവായി. വേണാട്ടുമുറ്റം ഉ്ണ്ണിക്കുട്ടന്‍ ശാസ്താം നടയ്ക്ക് സമീപത്തേക്കാണ് ഓടിയത്.രണ്ട് ആനകളെയും തളച്ചു.

 കീഴ്ശാന്തിമാര്‍ക്കും ചിലഭക്തര്‍ക്കും നിസാര പരിക്കുകള്‍ ഉണ്ട്.വൈകിട്ടത്തെ ശ്രീബലി എഴുന്നള്ളത്തിനിടയിലായിരുന്നു സംഭവം. രണ്ടാംവലത്തിന് ഗരുഡമാടത്തറയ്ക്ക് സമീപം എത്തിയപ്പോഴാണ് ആനവിരണ്ടത്.
പോലീസും അഗ്നിരക്ഷാസേനയും സ്ഥലത്തെത്തിയിട്ടുണ്ട്. നിലവിൽ ഭയപ്പെടേണ്ട സാഹചര്യമില്ല.

17/03/2025, 06:34 - Kannan: TITLE

Ectopic calcification:
new concepts in cellular regulation
17/03/2025, 06:34 - Kannan: Author 
C. M. Giachelli
17/03/2025, 06:34 - Kannan: Year : 2001
17/03/2025, 06:34 - Kannan: Species 

Mouse,rat, mice
17/03/2025, 06:34 - Kannan: INTRODUCTION 
Ectopic calcification refers to calcium salt crystal deposi-
tion in soft tissues. Ectopic calcification is a common
response to soft tissue injury and systemic mineral
imbalance, and can lead to devastating clinical conse-
quences especially when present in heart valves or blood
vessels as summarized in Table 1 (1–5). Furthermore,
ectopic calcification is recognized as a problem associ-
ated with biomaterial implantation and failure, especially
in cardiac valve bioprostheses, cardiac assist devices, and
intraocular lenses (6).
Until recently, the process of ectopic mineralization
was considered an unregulated and passive physico-
chemical process. In the past few years, however, a num-
ber of key observations have changed this perception.First, striking similarities between bone and ectopic
mineralization have been noted and are listed in Table 2
(7–20). Second, studies of mutated mice have led to the
identification of biomolecules responsible for genetic
control of ectopic mineralization, including matrix gla-
protein and osteopontin (Table 3) (21–27). Finally, his-
tological evidence for the presence of bone in advanced,
calcified atherosclerotic plaques, Monckeberg’s sclerosis,
and aortic stenosis has been reported (28–30). These
findings have bolstered the concept that ectopic calcifi-
cation is indeed a highly regulated, physiological host
response to injury and biomaterial implantation.Studies in my laboratory suggest that mesenchymal
and inflammatory cells normally maintain the balance
between pro-calcific and anti-calcific regulatory mole-
cules in tissues such that ectopic calcification is avoided.
Alteration in this balance induced by injury or bioma-
terial implantation is postulated to induce ectopic calci-
fication (Fig. 1). Current investigations, summarized
below, are devoted to identifying key nucleating as well
as anti-calcific mechanisms. These studies will open the
door for novel, rational approaches to limit, prevent, and
potentially reverse calcification of implanted biomate-
rials.
17/03/2025, 06:34 - Kannan: QUESTIONS 

1. What causes the imbalance between pro-calcific and anti-calcific molecules that leads to ectopic calcification in soft tissues?  

2. How can we use the knowledge of bone-like mineralization to prevent calcification in implanted biomaterials?
17/03/2025, 06:34 - Kannan: Paper 9 NOTES: Ecotopic calcification is a common response to soft tissue injury,which leads to devastating consequences if present in heart valve or blood vessels.Hypothesized that mesenchymal cells and inflammatory cells , normally maintain a balance between pro calcific and anti calcific regulatory proteins in soft tissue .
Developed in vivo and in vitro model of ectopic calcification and found elevated extracellular phosphate level induce smooth muscle culture mineralization morphologically similar to calcified human.
Sodium dependent phosphate cotransporter function is required for smooth muscle cell culture mineralization, which is associated with a dramatic loss of smooth muscle specific gene expression.
Osteopontin a secreted phosphoprotein abundant in macrophage found in human calcified atherosclerotic and valvular lesions is an inhibitor of ectopic calcification invitro and invivo.Furthermore ectopic calcification is recognised as a problem associated with biomaterial implantation and failure.Recent studies have changed the perspective of seeing ectopic calcification as an unregulated and passive physico chemical process .At first similarities between bones and ectopic mineralization have been noted,and then studies in mutated mice have led to identification of biomolecules responsible for genetic control of ectopic mineralization, including matrix gla protein and osteopontin.In conclusion studies suggest that mineralization of soft tissue depends on balance between active inducers and inhibitors.

11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: TITLE
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: Macrophage Heterogeneity Complicates Reversal of Calcification in Cardiovascular Tissues
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: ABSRTACT
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: Macrophages are highly heterogeneous cells exhibiting a wide range of protein markers, tissue locations, and functions. Often thought of as host defense cells with phagocytic, innate/adaptive immune system, and proinflammatory roles, macrophages contribute to a variety of tissue functions, including adipose thermogenesis, tissue repair, splenic and hepatic iron recycling, neural synaptic pruning, and cardiac electric conduction. In the current issue of Circulation Research, Chinetti-Gbaguidi et al1 enhance our understanding of the diverse roles of macrophages in vascular disease by reporting that macrophages near calcified regions of human atherosclerotic lesions display low mineral resorption potential. This study ties macrophage osteoclastogenesis to vascular calcification and identifies disrupted signaling pathways that may help to develop anticalcification therapies.
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: AUTHOR
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: Maximillian A. Rogers, Masanori Aikawa, and  Elena Aikawa
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: YEAR
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: 2017
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: NOTES
11/04/2025, 22:49 - Kannan: In human atherosclerosis (artery clogging disease),macrophages near calcified areas does not remove minerals ,so they dont break down calcium properly. This connects the way how macrophage act like osteoclast to artery calcification .It also showscertain broken pathways that might be useful target for new treatment.Macrophages are not just M1 and M2 ,they show a wide mix of behaviour ,even among M1 macrophage these are subtypes,this complexity makes vascular disease harder to fully understand and treat.Macrophages have harmful effect in clogged arteries ( atherosclerosis)in such a way it releases proinflammatory and toxic substances and secrete enzymes like MMPs that break down artery structure causing plaques to become unstable. These are some helpful roles like cleaning up cholesterol (lipoproteins) and dead cells and helps to end inflammation ,so that macrophage can be good and bad depending on type and action.

12/04/2025, 00:13 - Kannan: TITLE
12/04/2025, 00:13 - Kannan: Macrophage-Derived Matrix Vesicles
An Alternative Novel Mechanism for Microcalcification in
Atherosclerotic Plaques
12/04/2025, 00:14 - Kannan: AUTHOR
12/04/2025, 00:14 - Kannan: ophie E. P. New, Claudia Goettsch, Masanori Aikawa, Julio F. Marchini, Manabu Shibasaki,
Katsumi Yabusaki, Peter Libby, Catherine M. Shanahan, Kevin Croce, Elena Aikawa
12/04/2025, 00:15 - Kannan: YEAR :2013
12/04/2025, 00:15 - Kannan: ABSTRACT
12/04/2025, 00:17 - Kannan: Rationale: We previously showed that early calcification of atherosclerotic plaques associates with macrophage
accumulation. Chronic renal disease and mineral imbalance accelerate calcification and the subsequent release of
matrix vesicles (MVs), precursors of microcalcification.
Objective: We tested the hypothesis that macrophage-derived MVs contribute directly to microcalcification.
Methods and Results: Macrophages associated with regions of calcified vesicular structures in human carotid
plaques (n=136 patients). In vitro, macrophages released MVs with high calcification and aggregation potential.
MVs expressed exosomal markers (CD9 and TSG101) and contained S100A9 and annexin V. Silencing S100A9
in vitro and genetic deficiency in S100A9−/− mice reduced MV calcification, whereas stimulation with S100A9
increased calcification potential. Externalization of phosphatidylserine after Ca/P stimulation and interaction
of S100A9 and annexin V indicated that a phosphatidylserine-annexin V-S100A9 membrane complex facilitates
hydroxyapatite nucleation within the macrophage-derived MV membrane.
Conclusions: Our results support the novel concept that macrophages release calcifying MVs enriched in S100A9 and
annexin V, which contribute to accelerated microcalcification in chronic renal disease.
12/04/2025, 00:20 - Kannan: Questions:

12/04/2025, 00:27 - Kannan: Key Findings:
1.Macrophages are found near calcified areas in human artery plaques.
2.Macrophages release microvesicles (MVs) that have a high potential to cause calcification.

12/04/2025, 01:55 - Kannan: NOTES:                                                          Arterial micro calcification means tiny calcium deposition forming inside artery walls .These can appear in their cap that covers dead cells  areas inside atherosclerotic plaque ,these plaques form in inner layer of blood vessels .These tiny deposition of calcium cause change in stiffness ,increase local stress on artery walls ,plaque rupture which cause heart attack ,stroke and other acute cardiovascular events. Same plaque have spotty calcification which are small scattered calcium deposits these deposits came from calcified vesicles ,these increases stress ,making it more likely to break .People with chronic renal disease are more likely to get atherosclerosis (narrowing of arteries),often have calcification in both intima (inner layer) and media (middle layer) of arteries .Have a higher risk of heart related death. Chronic Renal Disease patients often have a high phosphate level in blood called hyperphosphatemia which triggers cells to release matrix vesicles ,which are tiny particles that cells release to start mineral building ,its a normal process and also appear in disease .Studies using molecular imaging found that macrophages (immune cells)appear together with calcification in artery walls. There is a new hypothesis ,smooth muscle cells become bone -like and cause calcification ,macrophage themselves might release matrix vesicles  that lead to micro calcification ,this means inflammation could directly cause artery calcification not just smooth muscle cells turning into bone like cells. <This message was edited>

12/04/2025, 02:06 - Kannan: TITLE
12/04/2025, 02:06 - Kannan: The shift of macrophages toward M1 phenotype promotes
aortic valvular calcification
12/04/2025, 02:06 - Kannan: AUTHOR
12/04/2025, 02:07 - Kannan: Geng Li, MD, PhD,a Weihua Qiao, MD, PhD,a Wenjing Zhang, MD,b Fei Li, MD,a Jiawei Shi, MD, PhD, a
and Nianguo Dong, MD, PhDa
12/04/2025, 02:08 - Kannan: YEAR : 2017
12/04/2025, 02:09 - Kannan: ABSTRACT :
Objective: The purpose of the present study was to comprehensively compare the
phenotype profile of infiltrated macrophages in human noncalcified and calcific
aortic valves, and to determine whether the shift of macrophage polarization
modulates valvular calcification in vitro.
Methods: Cell surface markers of macrophages and inflammatory cytokines
expression in 90 cases of human noncalcified and calcific aortic valve leaflets
were analyzed. The normal aortic valve interstitial cells were isolated and cultured
in vitro. After incubation with nonconditioned medium and conditioned medium
from unstimulated or lipopolysaccharide-stimulated U937 monocytes, valve
interstitial cells were evaluated by osteogenic differentiation markers.
Results: Infiltration of macrophages was enhanced in the calcific aortic valves,
and M1 phenotype was the predominant macrophage subsets. In addition, both
proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines were significantly upregulated
in the calcific aortic valves. Furthermore, lipopolysaccharide-stimulated
monocytes presented with increased expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase
and high proportional CD11c-positive (M1) macrophages. Conditioned medium
from unstimulated monocytes promoted the osteogenic differentiation of valve
interstitial cells in vitro, as evidenced by increased markers such as bone
morphogenetic protein 2, osteopontin, and alkaline phosphatase. Conditioned
medium from M1 macrophages further enhanced valve interstitial cells
calcification. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay showed that M1 phenotype
macrophages secreted tumor necrosis factors a and interleukin 6, and neutralizing
antibodies to these 2 proinflammatory cytokines attenuated induction of
osteogenic differentiation and calcification by the conditioned media.
Conclusions: Both total numbers and polarization of macrophage influence the
process of calcification in human aortic valve. The shift toward M1 phenotype
might promote valve interstitial cell calcification

12/04/2025, 03:57 - Gokul G J: Study aimed to compare types and behaviour of macrophages found in calcified and non calcified  human aortic valve. Ninety human aortic valve were studied ,some were normal (non calcified) and same were calcified (hardened )researchers looked at types of macrophages in the valve and also levels of inflammatory chemicals (cytokines)
The purpose of the study was to understand what kind of macrophage are found in healthy versus calcified aortic valve and also if these macrophages can change value cell and cause calcification. In the lab, valve interstitial cells were taken from healthy valves and grown in lab they were treated with normal liquid. Liquid from resting macrophages, liquid from activated M1 macrophages, and they checked whether the cells started turning into bone like cells. And they found calcified valves and more macrophages than healthy ones, most of these were M1 macrophages, there are pro-inflamatory, identified by CD11C marker. Both pro-inflamatory (like TNF-alpha) and IL-6 and anti-inflamatory cytokines were higher in calcified valves. Valvular intercells treated with liquid from activated macrophages showed more bone like changes, markers like BMB-2, osteponin and alkaline phosphate increase. M1 macrophages made, TNF-alpha and IL-6, and when it is blocked calcification was reduced. They concluded that the number and type of macrophages matter in valve disease, M1 macrophages helps start and increase calcification process and targeting changeing macrophages type may help, treat or prevent calcific aortic valve disease.

02/11/2025, 21:33 - Kannan: Aim:

To detect and estimate the presence of lipids (fats/oils) in oil samples and food materials (like poori) using the Sudan III staining method.

Principle:

Lipids are a heterogeneous group of compounds, including fats, oils, and waxes, which are insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents such as chloroform and ether. They are important biomolecules serving as energy reserves and structural components of cell membranes.

Sudan III is a fat-soluble lysochrome (dye) that selectively stains lipids. It is an orange-red dye that dissolves in non-polar substances like fats and oils but not in water. When a sample containing lipids is treated with Sudan III, the lipid components get stained red-orange, indicating the presence of fats.

The method is based on the solubility of lipids in organic solvents and their ability to bind to fat-soluble dyes such as Sudan III. When Sudan III is added to a sample containing lipids, the dye dissolves in the lipid portion, imparting a distinct orange-red color. The intensity of the color can give a qualitative or semi-quantitative estimate of lipid content.



Materials Required:

* Sudan III stain (prepared as 0.5% solution in alcohol or ethanol)
* Distilled water
* Test tubes
* Dropper or pipette
* Mortar and pestle (for crushing food sample)
* Filter paper
* Oil sample (e.g., groundnut oil, sunflower oil)
* Food sample (e.g., poori)
* Forceps or spatula


Preparation of Sudan III Stain:

* Dissolve **0.5 g Sudan III dye** in **100 mL of 70% ethanol.**
* Filter the solution to remove undissolved particles.
  (This forms a saturated solution of Sudan III.)


Procedure:
A. For Oil Sample:

1. Take a few drops of the oil sample in a clean test tube.
2. Add 2–3 drops of Sudan III stain.
3. Shake the mixture gently.
4. Observe the color change.

Observation:
An orange-red color develops in the oil layer, confirming the presence of lipids.



B. For Food Sample (Poori):

1. Crush a small piece of poori using mortar and pestle.
2. Add a small amount of the crushed poori to a test tube containing 2–3 mL of distilled water.
3. Add 2–3 drops of Sudan III stain and shake gently.
4. Allow it to stand for a few minutes.

Observation:
Red-orange stained oil droplets appear floating on the surface or within the food particles, indicating the presence of lipid/fat.

Result:

* **Oil sample:** Orange-red coloration observed → Lipid present.
* **Poori sample:** Orange-red stained droplets observed → Lipid present.


Conclusion:

Lipids were successfully detected in both the oil and poori samples using Sudan III stain. The red-orange coloration indicates the presence of fat or oil content in the tested materials.


Precautions:

* Sudan III stain should be handled carefully; avoid contact with skin.
* Use clean and dry glassware to avoid contamination.
* Shake the mixture gently to ensure uniform staining.
* Do not use too much stain, as it may obscure observation.

05/01/2026, 20:50 - Gokul G J: Presenter Notes: The Power of Fermentation

Slide 1: Title Slide (The Hook)

What to say: "Good morning everyone. Today, we are stepping into the invisible world of bioprocessing. We often think of factories as smoke-stacks and gears, but some of the most advanced manufacturing on Earth happens inside a single cell. I'm going to show you how we harness 'The Power of Fermentation' to solve global challenges."

Slide 2: What is Fermentation? (The Science)

What to say: "In simple terms, fermentation is life without air. It is an anaerobic metabolic pathway. While we breathe oxygen to make energy, microbes like yeast and bacteria can break down sugars to stay alive in environments where oxygen is scarce. For us, this isn't just a survival tactic; it’s a chemical bridge that turns simple sugar into high-value products like fuel, food, and medicine."

Slide 3: Our Microbial Partners (The Workers)

What to say: "We don't work alone. We have three main 'employees' in our bio-factories. First, Bacteria, the workhorses for organic acids. Second, Yeast, our oldest partners in brewing and baking, now used for biofuels. And finally, Fungi, which are essentially biological pharmacies, giving us life-saving antibiotics like Penicillin. Selecting the right 'worker' is the first step in any successful bioprocess."

Slide 4: The Industrial Workflow (The Logistics)

What to say: "How does this look in a factory? It’s a three-step journey. Upstream is the preparation phase—cooking the microbial 'soup' and making sure everything is sterile. The Process is where the magic happens inside the bioreactor. Finally, Downstream is the hardest part: it’s where we separate the tiny amount of product from the massive amount of waste. Think of it as finding a needle in a haystack, but the needle is worth millions."

Slide 5: Feeding Strategies (The Strategy)

What to say: "How we feed our microbes determines our profit. Batch is like a slow cooker; you put everything in and wait. It's simple but limited. Fed-Batch is the industry favorite; we add food slowly to keep the cells growing without overfeeding them. Continuous is the ultimate goal—a constant flow of production—but it’s like a marathon; one mistake or one 'bad' microbe can ruin the entire run."

Slide 6: Keeping Microbes Happy (The Environment)

What to say: "Microbes are sensitive. If the temperature is off by just 2 degrees, or the pH becomes too acidic, the 'factory' shuts down. We use sensors to act as the microbes' eyes and ears, adjusting oxygen and mixing speed in real-time. Our job as biotechnologists is essentially to be 'high-tech babysitters' for billions of cells."

Slide 7: Products for a Better World (The Impact)

What to say: "Why do we do this? Because fermentation saves lives. It’s how we make Insulin for diabetics. It’s how we make Bio-plastics that don't choke our oceans. And it’s how we create sustainable Agriculture to feed a growing population. We are moving away from oil-based chemistry toward a bio-based economy."

Slide 8: Yield Performance (The Data)

What to say: "If we look at the data, the 'Fed-Batch' method is the clear winner for efficiency. By controlling the feed rate, we can reach 90% of the theoretical maximum yield. In the industrial world, moving from a 45% batch yield to a 90% fed-batch yield can be the difference between a failed startup and a billion-dollar breakthrough."

Slide 9: The Future (The Vision)

What to say: "We are entering the era of Bio-Manufacturing 4.0. With AI and CRISPR gene editing, we aren't just using nature; we are optimizing it. We can now program cells to produce spider silk for clothing or lab-grown meat to reduce animal farming. The future of manufacturing isn't built; it's grown."

Slide 10: Q&A (The Interaction)

What to say: "Thank you for joining me on this journey through the bioreactor. I'd love to hear your thoughts or answer any questions you have about the future of fermentation."
